title: your grandmother before dinner
hookLine: your grandmother before dinner; a gift you didn't earn

lines: THE WORD IS BIGGER THAN THE SPEECH.
cards: The food is on the kitchen table, steam coming off the potatoes, and somebody's already reaching for the bread. Then a hand on the wrist. A grandmother, saying: wait.
Grace first. Heads go down. A few quick words, a quick amen, and everybody eats.
A kid at a table like that could grow up thinking grace means the little speech before dinner. It does. But the word is much bigger than the speech.
It's the reason for the speech.

teach.b: Grace comes from the Latin gratia: a favor, a gift, something given freely, not paid for. It's the same root that gives English gratitude, and gratis, free of charge.
The New Testament was written in Greek, and there the word is charis, which also means a gift freely given, and a kind of loveliness.
So when Catholics talk about grace, they mean God's gift of himself, given before anybody earned it.
The letter to the Ephesians says it plainly, in the Douay-Rheims Bible: "For by grace you are saved through faith, and that not of yourselves, for it is the gift of God." Not of yourselves.
That's the surprise at the heart of the word. You don't climb up to grace. It comes down to you.
Catholics say it arrives in many ways: in baptism and the other sacraments, in prayer, in an ordinary Tuesday when a friend calls at exactly the right moment.

teach.h: THE TABLE IS A SMALL PICTURE.
teach.b: Yesterday's small signs are there to get a person ready for it. And here's where the dinner table comes back in.

The traditional Catholic grace before meals goes: "Bless us, O Lord, and these thy gifts, which we are about to receive from thy bounty, through Christ our Lord. Amen." Listen to what it notices. Thy gifts.
Thy bounty. Somebody grew the food, somebody cooked it, and before any of that, Catholics say, somebody gave the world to begin with. So saying grace isn't paying a fee before eating.
It's noticing that you were given something.

how: Many Catholic families say a short grace before meals, often the traditional "Bless us, O Lord," and many make the sign of the cross before and after it.

games.q: what's inside the word — tap the pairs.

s: grace only means the words said before dinner
the words are named after the bigger thing: gratia, a gift freely given.
grace and gratitude come from the same root
both come from Latin gratia, a favor or gift.
in Catholic teaching, grace is earned by being good enough
"not of yourselves, for it is the gift of God." it comes first.

games.q: the letter to the Ephesians says people are saved by grace. where does it say grace comes from?
o: from being born into the right family.
games.why: "not of yourselves, for it is the gift of God." the whole point of the word is that it isn't earned.

practice: Here's the practice, and it's small on purpose. Think of one thing you have today that you didn't earn. The air, maybe.
A person. A roof. Let it come into focus, and stay with it while you breathe slowly.
If you pray, you can say thank you with each breath out. If you don't, just let yourself notice the gift.

wordCard.voice: Grace. A favor, a gift freely given. Catholics say it comes first, before anyone earns it. Eighth word.

orig.note: Greek: grace, favor, a gift freely given. Latin translated it gratia.

carryVoice: Your line: you are already held. Grace means the gift came first. That's day eight.
